stature.source: typical: the middle of the card's 30-70 m for San Francisco and Marin ravine stands (FEIS: trees over 61 m common on good sites); tall: Muir Woods' old trees; record: the tallest Muir Woods tree, about 258 ft (79 m, NPS). The species record, Hyperion, 115.9 m in Redwood National Park (Gymnosperm Database), is far north of this region and is not the truncation here; read 2026-11-04

roots.note: a fluted, buttressed base over a shallow root plate that spreads 15-30 m

targets.from: judgement values, no photographs measured: a stand-grown ravine redwood carries a narrow cone over a clear lower trunk (Gymnosperm Database: narrowly conic, becoming irregular with age; FEIS: self-prunes well in dense stands)

young.note: a dense, narrow spire, branches nearly to the ground; often one of a ring of sprouts around an old stump or root crown

old-growth.note: a giant: a buttressed, fluted red-brown column clear for half its height under a narrow, ragged crown, sometimes with several reiterated tops

description: The tallest tree on Earth, here a tall narrow spire in the fog-fed ravines of Marin and the Peninsula. Its thick, soft, red-brown bark comes away in long fibrous strips, and its flat sprays of dark needles make a deep, cool shade.

season_notes.winter: Rain drips through the dark sprays and tiny cones open along the twigs.
season_notes.spring: New shoot tips come in bright green against the old foliage.
season_notes.summer: Fog combs through the crowns and drips to the forest floor, the ravine stays cool and damp.
season_notes.fall: Old inner shoots brown and fall whole, carpeting the ground with rust-coloured litter.

range.where: fog-belt ravines, stream benches and north slopes of Marin, the San Francisco Peninsula and the Santa Cruz Mountains

notes: Grown from the Douglas-fir template because both are tall excurrent conifers with flat needles in sprays; what changes is the red-brown fibrous bark, a darker and narrower crown (a ravine redwood is a slim cone about a third as wide as it is tall), a heavier root flare, and old trees with a clear trunk to half their height. What the generator cannot express: the fluted, buttressed base of old trees, the burls, the fire-hollowed 'goosepens', the reiterated trunks in old crowns, and above all the ring of sprouts that rises around a fallen or burned parent (FEIS: root-crown sprouts can grow 2 m in a season and a root crown carries about five crop trees); a tile placing redwoods in clumps would show this better than one tree at a time. Foliage browse by black-tailed deer is light and mostly on sprouts; FEIS records no animal that feeds on the seed or foliage to any degree, and dusky-footed woodrats (not in the animal library) strip seedling bark. The old-growth class here tops at 79 m, the tallest measured tree in Muir Woods (NPS), not the 60-90 m of the north coast giants.
sources: Gymnosperm Database (conifers.org), Sequoia sempervirens, https://www.conifers.org/cu/Sequoia.php, read 2026-11-04
National Park Service, Muir Woods (tallest tree about 258 ft / 79 m), via search of nps.gov, read 2026-11-04
